📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his strategy for orbital data centers.

The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

Industry observers note that spaceX has said it aims to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people remarked. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

In a recent development, apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” stated Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he mentioned.

Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Newly introduced York.

Breaking: The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • It has been revealed that so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • Sources indicate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

It has been revealed that so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

Sources indicate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to promptly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed upgrade in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Recent findings suggest that external pressures and bugs in patches are not newly introduced, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” notes Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar problems elsewhere,” states Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

It has been revealed that still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In a recent development, in the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

Industry observers note that there are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik states. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

In a recent development, “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” states Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some organization data. The bank notes “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

Industry observers note that • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

Industry observers note that • Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPad Pro is Apple's best tablet, but not everyone needs its power.
  • According to recent reports, when choosing your next iPad, it's not a difficult decision if you know the base model works for your needs, or if you want a small tablet.
  • According to recent reports, the iPad Air starts at $749 for the 11-inch model with 128GB of storage and an M4 processor, while the 11-inch M5 256GB base iPad Pro costs $1,199.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPad Pro is Apple's best tablet, but not everyone needs its power.

According to recent reports, when choosing your next iPad, it's not a difficult decision if you know the base model works for your needs, or if you want a small tablet. But it's trickier to decide between the iPad Air and iPad Pro if you're using an iPad for work or creative pursuits. Is saving $450 and opting for the still-capable iPad Air something you'll regret in the future?

According to recent reports, the iPad Air starts at $749 for the 11-inch model with 128GB of storage and an M4 processor, while the 11-inch M5 256GB base iPad Pro costs $1,199. Both devices offer 13-inch variants if you want a larger screen. Those prices might seem higher than you remember, due to the ongoing RAM crisis that's been spiking consumer tech prices. Apple hasn't been immune to its effects, and has passed those costs onto would-be iPad customers.

While the iPad Pro packs plenty of improvements, its strongest selling point is what meets your eyes right away: the display. It also relies on a faster processor that makes a meaningful difference in intensive apps. Picking between it and the Air comes down to how you plan to take advantage of the Pro's advanced spec sheet.

The iPad Air's laminated IPS LED display is great, with solid color accuracy, P3 wide color gamut support and a pixel density of 264 ppi that makes text crisp and clear to read. The iPad Pro also has a pixel density of 264 ppi, but that's where the similarities end.

According to recent reports, at 1,000 nits and up to 1,600 nits with HDR, the Pro's brighter tandem OLED display is miles ahead of the Air's 500-nit display. It relies on two OLED panels stacked on each other to boost brightness and color accuracy. With a contrast ratio of 2,000,000:1, it has incredibly deep blacks, which are appreciated for video creation and consumption alike.

It has been revealed that its 120Hz ProMotion display also feels smoother as you work through app menus, play games or simply scroll through the interface. To conserve battery, it can drop down to 10Hz while displaying images or other static content like a webpage. To reduce reflections and hide smudges, Apple also offers a nano-texture glass option at an additional cost for the top-tier Pro models.

It has been revealed that the latest iPad Air released in March 2026 and relies on Apple's M4 chip, while the Pro stepped up to an M5 in October 2025. To put that in context, the iPad Pro lineup used M4 back in 2024. The M4 processor is more than enough for most tasks, including gaming and video editing. It can handle rendering, media editing and on-device AI tools with no problem.

However, we found that the M5 in the iPad Pro was twice as fast when it came to running local AI models for advanced image generation tools. It offers 45 percent higher graphics performance and 15 percent faster multithreaded performance over the M4 processor.

With the M5 chip, you'll shave off a couple of seconds across intensive tasks. Admittedly, these are niche use cases, but if you want the best hardware Apple offers, paying more for the Pro model saves you time across the experience. The uptick in performance also lets the iPad Pro drive external displays at 120Hz, while the Air is restricted to 60Hz.

While the camera is seldom on the priority list when considering an iPad, the iPad Pro relies on some nifty tech uncommon among tablets. A Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensor next to the Pro models' rear camera helps with better autofocus and AR scanning.

Sources indicate that through third-party apps like Polycam, it can make floor maps of your home and develop 3D renders. Apple's Measure app lets the iPad Pro accurately measure item heights and the distance between objects, making it a great assistant when you're getting newly introduced furniture or rearranging the house. While the iPad Air also has the Measure app, it lacks this sensor that enhances its accuracy.

On the front, the Pro supports Face ID, letting you unlock your tablet without a password, while the iPad Air still relies on a fingerprint sensor for Touch ID. The advanced TrueDepth camera array also grants the ability to develop a spatial render of your face for Animoji and Memoji, or Portrait Mode selfies with background blur adjustments.

The iPad Pro comes with twice the base storage (128GB vs. 256GB), plus quad speakers compared to the Air's stereo speaker setup. It also supports fast charging with a 60W power adapter (not included), while its Thunderbolt 3 / USB 4 USB-C port can transfer large files faster and drive external monitors at 120Hz. The Pros used to have more RAM than the Air models, but the M4 Air matches them with 12GB of unified memory.

The iPad Pro keeps these advantages in a body that's only 5.3mm (0.21 inches) deep, slimmer than the already impressive 6.1mm (0.24 inches) of the iPad Air. They offer the same 10 hours of battery life for web browsing and video streaming. Individually, these features may not mean much outside of specific purposes. But together, they can make a compelling argument for the cost.

Recent findings suggest that despite these advantages, there's not enough here for a casual user that would justify spending $450 more for the iPad Pro. At $749, the iPad Air strikes the right balance of performance and features despite Apple's price hike this year from its prior price of $599. If you aren't going to take advantage of the iPad Pro's extra horsepower for video and photo editing, or by making the iPad your primary work device, your needs will be served just as well by the more affordable iPad Air.

‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.
  • Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
  • Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

Sources indicate that “So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

Industry observers note that as of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

According to recent reports, dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he remarked, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Industry observers note that particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov stated – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” mentioned Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something fresh.”.

It has been revealed that it is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he remarked.

Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk.

Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (460 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the company's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
  • The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
  • Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the company's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.

The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

The proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.

The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most crucial in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.

Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

Industry observers note that "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.".

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.

"This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, said in a statement quoted by news agency AP.

He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics.".

"But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.".

Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

The hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.

In September, rival AI firm OpenAI mentioned its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

#81745. US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (5027 w)

US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (5027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
  • The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
  • Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also stated that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy prepares to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

Recent findings suggest that problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

In a recent development, that caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a new router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

Industry observers note that specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a latest Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

In a recent development, FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union noted that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

Similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

Industry observers note that to get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

(This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

It has been revealed that philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

In a recent development, as an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

Sources indicate that to kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

According to recent reports, and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

So you blueprint around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

According to recent reports, and even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

Industry observers note that it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

Sources indicate that L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a big network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

(Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

According to recent reports, so there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

Sources indicate that now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

Industry observers note that mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and states, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

So, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a newly introduced hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

Industry observers note that but this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

It’s important to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

Mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has stated that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

Ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

It has been revealed that but they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

It is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

Sources indicate that I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

Industry observers note that mann: An important caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

Recent findings suggest that but what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not remarked it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

It has been revealed that one of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

Industry observers note that so in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

In a recent development, do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that claims a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

That’s the first big thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

So it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the newly introduced router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

Industry observers note that then, and this is the important part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

Recent findings suggest that that may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

In a recent development, every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

It is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

You’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

Sources indicate that in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

Sources indicate that ars Technica: The router installation issue that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

Mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

It’s not that they don’t want to modernize, and it’s not like the FAA doesn’t want to modernize. It’s just that it’s the old squeaky wheel thing, right? The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

Actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live matter in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

According to recent reports, I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

Sources indicate that I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

It has been revealed that we could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

It has been revealed that mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. It decayed down to its essential mission, and preserved that essential mission at the expense of literally everything else.

The apparent lack of risk analysis is a very clear example of the worst case scenario. The network-spanning maintenance being done in the middle of the day and allowed to cascade as a failure into the entire NAS, that was horrible. So a single set of technologies failed, but the NAS itself showed its resilience in preserving that key mission all the way down to the minimum function, to the absolute zero, where the only piece left was just keep it safe. That’s what it’s supposed to do.

In a recent development, we don’t want to see it go that far down. We’d much rather have them just divert flights a couple minutes here and there. But if we need to get it all the way down to the only thing we have is safe aircraft, I’m good with that.

Industry observers note that ars Technica: Duffy is saying the FAA needs $50 billion to make sure this doesn’t happen again. And if I understood correctly, you were saying it is good to have support for enough funding for the FAA to do what it needs to do, even if Duffy tying it specifically to “this happened because we didn’t have enough money” is not necessarily the correct assessment.

Sources indicate that mann: Yeah. This happened because there wasn’t the right oversight. I’d be pretty confident to say that. If we just take $50 billion and throw it at the same people doing the same thing the same way, we don’t get a better system. We just get a whole bunch more of this.

In a recent development, because hiring more contractors and getting more routers replaced faster in the middle of the day with no risk assessment and incorrect configurations or however it came about… take some of that money and put it into oversight, put it into testing, and put it into whatever you need to do to make sure that however many more of these we’re going to do are done properly, and in this case, at 2 o’clock in the morning with a team of qualified people with the proper testing, people ready to pull a plug on it, all that kind of stuff. That’s money well spent.

Ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router matter that led to the ground stop. The FAA has remarked the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

Mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

Now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

It has been revealed that if you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

But you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

But the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

To the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

Industry observers note that SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and indicates, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

    #81741. Why does your phone say no service even with a SIM card?

    Why does your phone say no service even with a SIM card?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.
    • It has been revealed that the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry.
    • On your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.

    It has been revealed that the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry. Things like computers, game consoles and tablets will often find a way to alert you to an concern, which makes it easier to troubleshoot any potential problems that may arise.

    On your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does. Or if you do know what the SIM card does, it can lead to some worrying conclusions as you try to troubleshoot it.

    Fixing a SIM card error is a task that requires some diagnostic detective work, or if you're extra unlucky, some actual physical work. Thankfully, there are a lot of tools, both in your phone's settings and in the real world, that can assist with a potential fix.

    In a recent development, when a SIM card error leaves you without service, the phone will still work and power on; it will just be without its main features. The only thing that needs to be done is to take it out and put it right back in. This is usually caused by dropping the phone or ithe card not being properly seated when it was serviced for you, but you can use a SIM ejector tool to take it out. If you don't have one, something as simple as a paper clip or safety pin will usually do the trick.

    In a recent development, it's always worth finding out if it's something as simple as a carrier outage, which is entirely possible. If you have access to another device on a different carrier and it can connect to the internet or make a phone call, that could indicate a network outage specific to your carrier. Asking a local friend or family member using the same service whether their phone is working properly can confirm a carrier outage or eliminate it as a possibility.

    It has been revealed that your phone may be using an eSIM card, which replaces the physical card with a digital SIM. These are great, but they tend to have unique complications with international travel. If you're using an eSIM card, the way you access settings on an iPhone is slightly different from Android. On an iPhone, eSIM cards are located in Cellular or Mobile Data in the Settings menu, while Android stores them in a setting called SIM Manager. By turning on data roaming, you may fix any sort of problems you're having.

    A SIM card or "no service" error can sometimes be something at a software level as opposed to something being wrong with the card. One of the more common fixes is simply toggling airplane mode on and off. Airplane mode can be found by swiping down from the top of your phone and tapping the airplane button.

    You may also be able to do a quick network reset, which sounds bad but has zero effect on your personal files. Doing a network reset on an iPhone is largely similar to the process on Android. It should be noted, however, that the iPhone's network reset is in the Transfer or Reset section of Settings, while Android stores it in Reset Options, also in Settings. You will need to sign back into your Wi-Fi, however, along with some other connections.

    Recent findings suggest that we all get busy in life, and if you haven't paid your bill, then your SIM card will simply stop connecting to your carrier's network. It may seem like a simple thing, but sometimes the simple solutions are blindingly obvious. If you pay your bill online, check your account to see if you've missed a payment or if your service hasn't been suspended for some other reason.

    According to recent reports, getting no service on your phone may not even have anything to do with a bad SIM card or an inactive account. You may just be in a place with limited to no service available, or a cellphone tower may be blocked by something. Move around and look for someplace that you actually can connect, as the error may be a result of poor service in that area.

    Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All options open in future talks, indicates Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’.
    • The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.
    • The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All options open in future talks, indicates Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’.

    The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.

    The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.

    Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.

    Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

    Recent findings suggest that miliband stated Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.

    However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

    Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”.

    Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.

    Burnham has previously noted he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

    The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.

    Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.

    It has been revealed that “Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he stated. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”.

    He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

    Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

    The foreign secretary mentioned: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”.

    On Friday, Burnham remarked the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

    Recent findings suggest that “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

    Recent findings suggest that the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she remarked: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”.

    Sources indicate that the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”.

    #81738. Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's a rundown of some Google tools that ended up in the graveyard this year.
    • According to recent reports, google is inherently data-driven, and that extends to its products and services as well.
    • According to recent reports, google Assistant has been phased out in favor of Gemini on mobile devices.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here's a rundown of some Google tools that ended up in the graveyard this year.

    According to recent reports, google is inherently data-driven, and that extends to its products and services as well. The search giant has a tendency to shut down services when it feels they're not serving its broader goals, and this has led to the discontinuation of products as diverse as Google Reader, Google+, Stadia, Google Glass, Google Hangouts and dozens of other utilities over the last 15 years. 2026 is no different, so let's take a look at everything Google discontinued this year.

    According to recent reports, google Assistant has been phased out in favor of Gemini on mobile devices. Google initially targeted the end of 2025 for the transition, but pushed the deadline to September, 2026. This means Assistant is no longer available on mobile devices, Wear OS smartwatches, headphones and earbuds, or vehicles using Android Auto projected from a user's phone. It's still usable on older devices like Nest Audio, Nest Mini, the original Google Home, Google Home Max and cars with Google built-in.

    It has been revealed that google Assistant debuted in 2016 (in the short-lived chat app Allo, of all things), and was integrated into much of the broader Android ecosystem, including mobile phones, tablets, smart home devices and vehicles. It provided a hands-free way to control smart home lights, play music, call contacts, and look up information on the web. Those tasks will now be handled by Gemini.

    It has been revealed that the Pixel Tablet was discontinued in September 2026; the link to its listing now takes you to the Google Store's home page, and Google removed tablets as a category from its site navigation. Google's tablet ambitions have felt half-hearted at times, but the Pixel Tablet sought to change that. The tablet debuted in 2023 for $499, and it came with an 11-inch 60Hz LCD panel, decent hardware and reliable battery life. Google sold the tablet for as little as $250 during the 2025 Black Friday sale.

    It has been revealed that its key selling point was the included Charging Speaker Dock, which effectively turned the tablet into a Nest Hub Max. The dock contained a dedicated speaker and served as a Cast target, allowing people to cast music and podcasts to the device. With the discontinuation of the Pixel Tablet, Google no longer has a tablet of its own; there were leaks pointing to a successor with a 120Hz panel, but that never materialized. With Google now focusing on Googlebooks, it may be a while before we see another Pixel Tablet.

    Google ended production of the Nest Mini and Nest Audio in June 2026, with both products now discontinued. The Nest Mini proved particularly popular after Google announced it in 2019 for just $50, and the smart speaker offered an affordable way to interact with Google Assistant and play music or control smart home devices.

    Nest Audio debuted in 2020 for $99, serving as the successor to the original Google Home. It featured a fabric design and surprisingly solid audio quality via two drivers — a 75mm woofer and 19mm tweeter — with only the much larger and more expensive Home Max rivaling its sound quality in Google's speaker portfolio.

    Even though the Nest Audio and Nest Mini are discontinued, Google will continue providing software updates for the foreseeable future. Google is now positioning the $99 Google Home Speaker as the go-to choice for anyone looking for a smart speaker. The Home Speaker has 360-degree sound, but it comes with a smaller 58mm driver, and features Gemini instead of Google Assistant.

    It has been revealed that as part of a broader rebranding initiative centered around Google Health, Google turned the Fitbit app into a unified health portal in May 2026. Alongside the change, Google also indicated that it was migrating Google Fit data over to Google Health.

    Google is positioning Health as its go-to choice to monitor health and fitness data from existing Fitbit wearables, and newer devices like the Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge use it from the get-go. Fitbit's Web APIs have also been wound down, so if you're using a Fitbit fitness band or smartwatch, you will need to install and use Google Health to monitor metrics. While Health has a lot of features — including an AI-assisted Health Coach — it lacks the social features that made Fitbit's app stand out.

    In January 2026, Google confirmed that it was ending the service, noting that it didn't "provide helpful next steps," and that it would instead focus on "tools that give you more clear, actionable steps to protect your information online." While there are other monitoring services such as Have I Been Pwned, Google's Dark Web Report was notable because it was integrated into your Google account.

    Gmailify was a feature that let you use Yahoo, AOL or Outlook email accounts with Gmail and access spam protection, search, automatic sorting and other services available within Google's email service. The feature debuted 10 years ago, but it was discontinued in Q1 2026; existing owners will still be able to use it until January 2027, and then it will be wound down.

    That remarked, Google still lets you access email from third-party accounts within Gmail for Android and iOS, and it uses the standard Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) protocol to fetch mails. The only glitch is that you don't get some of the extras, like spam protection. In a similar move, Google ended the ability to fetch emails from third-party accounts using the Post Office Protocol (POP); you'll have to use the newer IMAP standard to sync your mails going forward.

    In a recent development, in addition to these, Google discontinued several lesser-known initiatives in 2026. Google confirmed in July 2026 that the legacy Google Earth Pro desktop app would no longer be available to download after June 25, 2027. If you've used Google Earth Pro in the past and want to continue using it, all you need to do is download and install the app before June 2027, and it will continue to work even after the wind-down. Google is moving its focus to Google Earth on the web and Android/iOS, and while you can still view satellite imagery and Street View for free, it is introducing tiered subscription prepares for access to additional data layers.

    In a recent development, also, Steam for Chromebooks, a beta program that allowed people to install Steam games on ChromeOS machines, ended in January 2026. Google shut down Pixel Studio, a dedicated app that debuted with the Pixel 9 series and let you create AI-assisted imagery using text prompts, in March 2026. With image generation moving to Gemini, Google is directing users to its latest AI assistant instead. Google clearly likes building new tools and features, and while that means there's always something exciting on the horizon, the downside is that there's no guarantee the service you use today will be available a year or two down the line.

    #81735. Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (438 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve remarked it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost.
    • “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday.
    • It has been revealed that if Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good tech giant.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve remarked it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost problems will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

    “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

    It has been revealed that if Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good tech giant. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

    For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.

    According to recent reports, while Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

    In a recent development, for now, at least, Valve says it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

    Valve states it looks to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.
