    #81685. Industry News: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (822 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.
    • The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage.
    • According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

    The data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

    According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

    The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

    Industry observers note that sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the manufacturer to the issue, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

    Sources indicate that sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”.

    Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

    Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

    In a recent development, “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, mentioned in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”.

    “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

    The organization said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

    It’s unclear if the manufacturer has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

    According to recent reports, discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

    The modern web runs on absolute trust, he stated, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

    Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen remarked that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

    “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

    Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the latest wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

    Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

    “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”.

    #81682. ‘No time for a culture war’: Victoria’s electricity supply is at risk. Can it avoid power shortages and bill shocks?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1127 w)
    📖 Baca

    ‘No time for a culture war’: Victoria’s electricity supply is at risk. Can it avoid power shortages and bill shocks?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • State faces electricity supply gap when Yallourn coal-fired power station closes in 2028 as experts warn neither Labor nor the Coalition has adequate prepares.
    • Victoria’s electricity supply will be at risk when a major power plant shuts in 2028 and neither major party is offering a proposal at this month’s state election to deal with it, experts have warned.
    • In a recent development, all parties concede the giant Yallourn coal plant, which has operated in the Latrobe Valley since the 1970s and supplies a fifth of Victoria’s energy, is at the end of its functional life and will shut in less than two years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    State faces electricity supply gap when Yallourn coal-fired power station closes in 2028 as experts warn neither Labor nor the Coalition has adequate prepares.

    Victoria’s electricity supply will be at risk when a major power plant shuts in 2028 and neither major party is offering a proposal at this month’s state election to deal with it, experts have warned.

    In a recent development, all parties concede the giant Yallourn coal plant, which has operated in the Latrobe Valley since the 1970s and supplies a fifth of Victoria’s energy, is at the end of its functional life and will shut in less than two years. Analysts say the parties vying to run the state are failing to properly explain how they will fill the power shortfall the closure will create.

    The challenge facing Victoria is exacerbated by the growth in energy demand from datacentres and the electrification of buildings, homes and vehicles. Experts are most critical of the Coalition, under Liberal leader Jess Wilson, which is favoured to win the election. It claims it would stop work on new transmission lines – the high-voltage power lines needed to connect new wind and solar farms and allow Victoria to import power from neighbouring states.

    Tim Baxter, of consultancy Naru Research, says there is no “time for a culture war on energy in Victoria” because poor choices now would be “devastating” for the state’s economy and create bill shocks for households and businesses.

    According to recent reports, he indicates cheap gas helped build Victoria’s past prosperity, but it is swiftly running out with offshore gas supply from Bass Strait in steep decline. And there is no evidence the state has meaningful gas resources elsewhere to replace it. This has contributed to a 62% increase in gas prices in five years, he says, while electricity bills have risen by 18%.

    Given Victorians rely more on gas than other states, Baxter says it underlines the need for households to move away from gas and increasingly run on renewable energy. “Every windfarm, solar farm and battery that comes online before 2028 reduces how much expensive gas Victoria has to burn when Yallourn goes. That makes speeding up the build-out the single best way to protect households from higher bills,” he says.

    It has been revealed that victoria’s wholesale electricity prices are the lowest on the east coast, but households still rely heavily on expensive gas. Regardless of who wins, energy bills are likely to increase, according to a government briefing reported in the Herald Sun.

    In a recent development, the Coalition notes it would scrap VNI West, a transmission line linking Victoria to Upcoming South Wales, and pause work on the Western Renewables Link, between Melbourne and the state’s west. Instead, it would undertake a “short, sharp and independent” review of the state’s transmission strategy, which would consider alternatives, such as solar power on commercial and industrial rooftops.

    It has also pledged to “throw open the doors to gas exploration”, reverse Labor’s policy of making latest homes all-electric, and tender for new firming capacity with an Energy Security Requirement modelled on schemes in NSW and South Australia. There is no plan to change the state’s emission reduction targets – cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 75%–80% below 2005 levels by 2035 and reaching net zero emissions by 2045 – but it has not said how it would achieve them.

    Labor states it would continue to expand the power grid, shift homes from gas to electricity for heating and cooking and continue to support the development of offshore windfarms. But the Carroll government is also reviewing the Western Renewables Link. It recently cancelled a renewable energy zone, approved two gas developments (although one has since entered administration), and announced $7.5m to kickstart a “renewable gas industry”.

    Recent findings suggest that nexa Advisory chief executive Stephanie Bashir notes latest transmission is crucial for developing renewable energy and allowing power to be imported across state lines at times of high demand, such as during heatwaves. “This is not the time to be cancelling any of the projects in the pipeline,” she says. “This is the time where we put our foot on the accelerator and go hard.”.

    Environment Victoria’s chief executive, Jono La Nauze, says the Coalition’s proposal – including a proposal to reinstate a policy introduced by the previous Baillieu-Napthine Coalition government preventing wind turbines being built within 2km of dwellings – is “the greatest swindle ever attempted on Victorian voters”.

    “The Coalition are promising to stop all the things that are necessary to replace our coal and gas generation. They’ve got some quick slogans for how they’re going to instead rely on gas, with absolutely no substance,” he states.

    But analysts say Labor is also not building energy infrastructure fast enough.

    Oliver Nunn, managing director of the consultancy Endgame Analytics, claims the lack of an adequate strategy to stave off an energy shortfall means that “whoever wins [the election], we lose”.

    “You can see demand for electricity pulling up rapidly in Victoria, 5% year-on-year growth,” Nunn says. “Coal’s going out, and we just do not have, at this point, a really viable initiative.”.

    In a recent development, in its 12 years in government, Labor has overseen a surge in Victoria’s share of renewable energy from 10% to 44% and the closure of the large Hazelwood coal-fired power station. The number of windfarms has grown from 14 to 44 and large-scale solar farms from two to 57. Labor also ended the state’s moratorium on conventional gas exploration in 2021.

    But the state’s auditor general notes both VNI West and the Western Renewables Link are behind schedule, and not likely to be completed until after Yallourn’s scheduled closure.

    According to recent reports, recent attempts to fast-track the process by legislating for compulsory land acquisition before environmental approvals have been unpopular in regional communities, but Labor says the changes were needed to reduce delays and improve certainty for landowners. Controversially, Labor also passed laws to allow VicGrid and its contractors access to private land without a landholder’s consent, as a last resort to facilitate works.

    “Every time the government seems to hit a hurdle, what they’ve done is not gone back and reassessed the engagement and tried to improve it, what they’ve done is changed legislation to give them broader powers,” the Victorian Farmers Federation president, Ryan Milgate, says.

    The shadow energy minister, David Davis, refers to the laws as Labor’s “double bazooka powers” and says the Coalition will ditch them and reinstate landholder appeal rights.

    But Nexa’s Bashir indicates energy policy should not be “a political football”.

    According to recent reports, “We do need to back the replacement generation. We can’t do any more reviews; we’ve just got to get on with it.”.

    Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week.

    As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

    It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

    Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

    Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet firm. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

    Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

    Recent findings suggest that flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

    Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

    Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the tech giant has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

    “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

    #81676. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
    • Industry observers note that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
    • Patch, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

    Industry observers note that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end owners and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

    Patch, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and stated that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

    In a recent development, to test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

    Industry observers note that the findings are striking. They included:.

    “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

    In a recent development, although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

    The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

    Industry observers note that each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

    Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM consumers to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

    Industry observers note that secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were promptly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

    According to recent reports, as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

    In a recent development, last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

    Sources indicate that the clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

    It has been revealed that this wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

    The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

    Recent findings suggest that the blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

    • Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

    Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

    The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

    Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

    Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

    Sources indicate that the S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

    The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

    Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

    Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

    The artificial intelligence (AI) organization's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

    Analysts remarked volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

    Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI manufacturer experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

    Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

    While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

    "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

    "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability.".

    Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

    Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

    In a recent development, musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the organization noted was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

    But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

    Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

    Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

    Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

    Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

    South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

    Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

    Breaking: Victorian Greens win injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instructed people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party.
    • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • The Victorian Greens have won a supreme court injunction to stop an independent candidate from handing out how to vote cards that mimic their branding and urge people to preference it last.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instructed people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party.

    Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

    The Victorian Greens have won a supreme court injunction to stop an independent candidate from handing out how to vote cards that mimic their branding and urge people to preference it last.

    The decision has been welcomed by the party’s leader, Ellen Sandell, who noted the flyers distributed by people wearing the exact same colour shirts as genuine Greens volunteers had already misled voters.

    “The last thing people need when they walk into a polling booth is dodgy how-to-vote material designed to trick them into voting the exact opposite way they intended,” Sandell stated.

    The decision comes after Guardian Australia confirmed that people handing out material for the independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan were initially offered $25 an hour to do so.

    As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

    The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

    Sources indicate that the Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

    On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

    Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

    “Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card remarked.

    But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

    At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. He told the court the flyers were designed to mislead voters.

    “There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

    Guardian Australia has confirmed an ad on Airtasker offering payment to those handing out flyers at pre-poll in Prahran was for Finnegan’s campaign.

    “I need people to hand out flyers at election booths in Prahran and Richmond $25 per hour during the day from 18-28 November,” the ad said.

    But the person who published the ad, Finnegan’s friend Dean Hurston, said no one was recruited through Airtasker as Finnegan had found volunteers elsewhere.

    Justice John Watson granted the injunction on both how-to-vote cards on Sunday morning, after hearing testimony from the Victorian Electoral Commission on Saturday afternoon.

    Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to promptly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

    “It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

    Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print newly introduced cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

    “I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

    “The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”.

    On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

    Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

    A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

    It has been revealed that finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

    According to recent reports, the former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

    • Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on massive tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
    • The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.

    Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on massive tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

    The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

    A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

    Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

    But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s newly introduced draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing.".

    The proposal includes a string of fresh "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

    The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

    Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

    Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

    Industry observers note that neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's proposal will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

    According to recent reports, "This is a realistic budget that addresses our latest priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement.".

    But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

    The French presidency stated the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers.".

    "As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement.".

    The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
    • The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
    • Recent findings suggest that those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

    The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

    But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the manufacturer’s orbital data center prepares. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

    That may not matter to the organization in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

    However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the firm failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

    Recent findings suggest that even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

    That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

    A police officer who was shot outside a remote Tasmanian police station is alleged to have shot and killed his attacker in response to what authorities believe was a “targeted” incident.

    Industry observers note that tasmania police deputy commissioner, Jonathan Higgins, mentioned the sergeant had just come off shift at Whitemark police station on Flinders Island, which is north-east of the Tasmanian mainland. He had parked and gotten out of his police vehicle when he was shot at about 9.45pm on Saturday, Higgins told reporters on Sunday.

    Investigators sent to investigate the shooting of the sergeant discovered the body of a man, aged in his mid-20s, on Walker Street a few hundred metres from the police station.

    Police believe he was shot by the sergeant, who fired his weapon a number of times.

    “At this early stage in the investigation, police believe this was a targeted incident,’” Higgins said.

    On Sunday afternoon the sergeant was in the operating theatre undergoing surgery at the Royal Hobart hospital and remained in a serious but stable condition.

    He is one of three officers stationed on Flinders Island and has worked there for a number of years.

    Whitemark has a population of about 300 according to the 2021 census, and the entire population of Flinders Island is fewer than 1,000 people.

    Extra police resources, including forensic and uniformed officers, have been deployed to the island. Those with information about these incidents, including CCTV or dashcam footage of Walker Street, have been urged to contact police.

    Police are hoping to speak to the family of the deceased man.

    Higgins said it was “the nature of our work” for police to receive threats from the public.

    The Tasmanian premier, Jeremy Rockliff, has been in contact with the state’s police commissioner, Donna Adams, who attended the Hobart hospital as the shot sergeant undergoes treatment.

    “My thoughts are with everyone affected by this horrific incident, including the police officer, their family and colleagues,” Rockliff mentioned.

    “Our police officers work every single day to keep Tasmanians safe, and incidents like this are a stark reminder of the risks they face in the line of duty.”.

    In a recent development, it is the second shooting of an on-duty police officer in Tasmania in 18 months. A Tasmanian officer was killed in the state’s north-west in June 2025 while executing a court-issued warrant to repossess a residence. The occupant of the home pleaded guilty to murder.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
    • The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio.

    Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

    The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

    Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

    Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

    Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

    All were told they could never serve in the police again.

    In a recent development, the case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

    Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

    It has been revealed that this was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

    Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

    The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

    It has been revealed that the incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

    According to recent reports, they later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

    After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

    Sources indicate that the officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

    During the trial Zecler mentioned had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

    In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux noted he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

    China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.
    • China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
    • The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it remarked was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.

    China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

    The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it remarked was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

    The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

    The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

    “We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”.

    Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

    In a recent development, some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

    The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

    Industry observers note that “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

    Analysts had noted that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

    In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

    According to recent reports, first among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and revealed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”.

    Industry observers note that the declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

    Sources indicate that hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”.

    It has been revealed that xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

    Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

    European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

    The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was vital, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

    Industry observers note that trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi mentioned the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

    It has been revealed that another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi noted the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

    According to recent reports, ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

    Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks.
    • The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public.
    • In a recent development, geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

    The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

    In a recent development, geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

    An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

    Sources indicate that the secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

    It has been revealed that super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy stated on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

    In a recent development, google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the manufacturer’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

    Sources indicate that meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy revealed it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

    XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

    Recent findings suggest that quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the organization will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

    Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

    The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

    In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

    Industry observers note that investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

    Recent findings suggest that as with any latest technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

    That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

    The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
    • The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
    • Recent findings suggest that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

    The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

    Recent findings suggest that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    According to recent reports, xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

    After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

    The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.

    Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceCompact.

    Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

    Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceExtended dynamic range.

    Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

    It has been revealed that there are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

    They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

    Recent findings suggest that the rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

    You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

    In a recent development, unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

    Industry observers note that the only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

    It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

    Industry observers note that xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a latest third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other massive Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

    In a recent development, the ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

    Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.

    The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

    California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors.
    • California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
    • Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based organization’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors.

    California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

    Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based organization’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

    “The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” noted Bonta.

    “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”.

    The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

    Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.

    Megaspeed has noted it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

    Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

    “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he stated. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”.

    Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

    Industry observers note that earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, stated the firm had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.

    Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

    Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

    The organization, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

    Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

    AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

    “AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the organization mentioned. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”.

    AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

    Watch: Miliband spoke to the BBC following the summit in Brussels.

    A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

    The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a latest youth mobility scheme.

    However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

    European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

    Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband remarked "all the options will be on the table".

    It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

    What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

    Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more.

    Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow.

    UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

    The prime minister mentioned the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.

    EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

    Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

    "President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She mentioned there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate concern, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

    Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary mentioned: "Yes, absolutely.".

    "The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely.".

    Miliband mentioned there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no latest contributions to the EU budget.

    He mentioned previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

    Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

    Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

    He stated that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

    "Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

    Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch mentioned the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

    She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

    Reform UK leader Nigel Farage mentioned Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

    Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud.".

    Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey stated there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

    It has been revealed that "A youth mobility scheme is a substantial step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast.".

    Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison mentioned closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the glitch of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".

    He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".

    He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway.".

    Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle stated the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.
